transcript: I have worked across the aisle to champion bipartisan support in Congress for the strategic defeat of Russia in Ukraine. The United States needs to lead the world in upholding the post-war rules-based order, and I think Greeks can well appreciate how important that post-World War II rules-based order has been for spreading peace and prosperity ever more widely. And we also need to send a message to the authoritarian regime in Moscow and Beijing as well that might does not make right. And the United States is going to stand with freedom and democracy when it is under duress. I think exceeding almost everybody's expectations, the Ukrainians have fought with a courage and an ingenuity that has got the Russians back on their heels. We need to continue to provide sustained military and material support to the Ukrainian fighters so that they can continue their advance in the northeast as well as the south. We also need to provide humanitarian and economic aid so they can keep their economy going and prevent the worst suffering. And we've got to continue to strangle the Russian economy with central bank, commercial, and most importantly, energy sanctions. That's the trifecta. We've already done the central bank sanctions. They were effective. The commercial sanctions are going to bite increasingly hard in 2023 and 2024 in preventing the Russian avionics and maritime and military and semiconductor and electronics industries from being able to replenish their stock. But the energy sanctions are the most important right now because The Kremlin has been funding this illegal war with the hard currency of their oil and natural gas shipments, particularly oil. For that reason, I've led a bipartisan letter to Treasury in support of the G7's proposed price caps on Russian oil, which would do two things. I won't get into all the mechanics of it, but basically it would lower prices for Western energy consumers, while also depriving the Kremlin of market rate hard currency for their oil shipments. It's a win-win requires a strong diplomatic international effort. If we can pull it off, it would be a tremendous blow for Ukraine in favor of their defense of the homeland. We need to stand with Ukraine for this winter coming up. It's going to be a hard winter. I'm not going to sugarcoat it. It's going to be a hard winter for the Ukrainians who are fighting on the front lines. It's going to be a hard winter for the Europeans who are dealing with exorbitantly high energy bills. And it's going to be a tough winter also, potentially for the United States. We're also going to face higher energy bills and potentially higher food bills and a pinching economy. But there are some things worth sacrificing for, and the free world is one of them.
